scams.name: Bird Droppings Pickpocket Scam
scams.description: You’re walking along the promenade near Grande Plage when suddenly something white and sticky lands on your shoulder. You look up instinctively, thinking it’s bird droppings. Immediately, a ‘helpful’ local appears, tutting at the pigeons and offering to help clean you up. While you’re distracted and they’re wiping your shoulder, their accomplice is emptying your pockets or bag. The ‘droppings’ are actually white paste thrown by a confederate.
scams.avoidance: If substance lands on you, step away from any ‘helpers’ and handle it yourself. Say ‘Non, merci, ca va’ (No thanks, I’m fine) and move to a shop or restaurant to clean up. Keep wallet in a front pocket or secure crossbody bag that can’t be accessed while you’re distracted. Be suspicious of any ‘helpful stranger’ appearing instantly after an unexpected mishap.
scams.location: Streets near Grande Plage, Promenade du Casino, Avenue Edouard VII, pedestrian areas in city center

scams.name: Beach Blanket Theft at Grande Plage
scams.description: You’ve found a perfect spot on the golden sands of Grande Plage and left your bag and belongings on your beach towel while going for a quick swim in the Atlantic. In those few minutes, a thief has been watching and waiting. They casually stroll past your blanket, scoop up your phone, wallet, and keys in one fluid motion, and disappear into the crowd before you’ve even noticed. Beach theft spikes during July and August.
scams.avoidance: Never leave valuables unattended on the beach — use a waterproof pouch to take essentials into the water. Leave passport, excess cash, and electronics in your hotel safe before heading to the beach. Swim in shifts with companions so someone always watches belongings. Position yourself near lifeguard stations where surveillance is higher.
scams.location: Grande Plage, Plage Miramar, Cote des Basques, beach areas during peak summer season

scams.name: Camera Drop Scam
scams.description: You’re admiring the stunning view from Rocher de la Vierge when a friendly tourist asks if you’d take their photo with their nice-looking camera. You oblige, and as you hand the camera back, they fumble it dramatically and it crashes to the ground. They examine their ‘broken’ camera and start demanding you pay for the damage — €200-300 or more. The camera was already broken or is a cheap prop.
scams.avoidance: It’s fine to take photos for tourists, but hand the camera back carefully and step back before releasing. If they drop it, remember the fumble was on their end. Never pay cash on the spot; suggest involving police if they claim damage. Walk away if they become aggressive.
scams.location: Rocher de la Vierge viewpoint, Port Vieux, Grande Plage promenade, popular photo spots

scams.name: ATM Card Skimming and Shoulder Surfing
scams.description: You’re withdrawing cash from an ATM near the casino when someone approaches offering helpful advice about fees. While they ‘help,’ they’re watching you enter your PIN and may have a card skimmer in their pocket scanning your card’s magnetic strip. Or they’ve already installed a skimmer on the ATM slot itself. Days later, your account shows unauthorized withdrawals in eastern Europe.
scams.avoidance: Use ATMs inside banks during business hours where tampering is less likely. Cover the keypad completely with your hand when entering your PIN. Check the card slot by wiggling it gently — skimmers are often loosely attached. Never accept help from strangers at ATMs.
scams.location: ATMs near Casino Barriere, Avenue Edouard VII, Les Halles market area, train station

scams.name: Shell Game and Three-Card Monte
scams.description: You spot a small crowd gathered around a man with three boxes or cards on a folding table near the casino promenade. He’s shuffling them rapidly, inviting people to guess which one hides the ball. Someone in the crowd bets €20 and wins easily. But those ‘winners’ are accomplices working with the operator. The moment you put money down, sleight of hand ensures you lose. Meanwhile, pickpockets work the crowd.
scams.avoidance: Never gamble with street operators — the games are rigged without exception. Walk past quickly without stopping to watch; observation makes you a target. Remember that every ‘winner’ you see is a plant working with the scammer. Keep hands on your valuables if you even pause near a street game.
scams.location: Casino promenade, Grande Plage boardwalk, near Rocher de la Vierge during peak tourist season

scams.name: Friendly Bar Overcharging Scam
scams.description: You’re enjoying an evening when two attractive locals strike up a friendly conversation and suggest drinks at a place they know nearby. After a couple of drinks, the bill arrives: €150-200 or more for what seemed like a few cocktails. The drinks were massively inflated ‘tourist prices,’ and your ‘friends’ chip in only a token amount before disappearing. Large bouncers may escort you to an ATM if you protest.
scams.avoidance: Choose your own venues — never let strangers guide you to a bar they recommend. Always check prices before ordering; no posted prices is a massive red flag. Suggest well-known, established bars if new acquaintances want drinks. If confronted with an outrageous bill, insist on calling police before paying.
scams.location: Bars near Port Vieux, late-night establishments in city center, venues off main tourist streets

scams.name: Les Halles Market Pickpocketing
scams.description: Les Halles is a beloved Biarritz institution where locals and tourists jostle to buy fresh seafood and regional specialties. The crowded aisles, sensory overload, and tourists fumbling with euros make it a prime hunting ground for skilled pickpockets. While you’re admiring the piment d’Espelette display or counting change, a bump passes unnoticed — and your wallet goes with it.
scams.avoidance: Wear a crossbody bag with the opening against your body, hand resting on top. Keep wallet in a front pocket, never in a backpack or rear pocket. Bring only the cash you need for market purchases; leave cards at the hotel. Be extra vigilant during peak Saturday morning hours.
scams.location: Les Halles de Biarritz indoor market, Saturday morning market, Rue des Halles area

scams.name: Unlicensed Taxi Overcharging
scams.description: You’ve just landed at Biarritz Airport after a long journey, and as you exit arrivals, a friendly man approaches offering a taxi into town. He quotes €40 — but this isn’t an official taxi. Once in the car, the price might increase, or you’re taken on a scenic route. Official airport taxis should cost around €25 to central Biarritz. Unlicensed operators charge double or triple the standard fare.
scams.avoidance: Use only official taxis from the designated taxi rank at the airport or station. Look for official taxi signage, license numbers on windshield, and running meters. Know the expected fare in advance: airport to city center is approximately €25. Use ride-hailing apps for transparent pricing.
scams.location: Biarritz-Pays Basque Airport (BIQ), Biarritz train station, late-night casino area

scams.name: Fake Charity Petition Scam
scams.description: You’re strolling along the promenade when a young woman approaches with a clipboard, gesturing that she’s deaf-mute. She wants you to sign a petition for disabled children or another worthy cause. Once signed, she flips to a donation page showing €20-50 amounts. Meanwhile, your attention is on the clipboard, making you an easy mark for an accomplice to pickpocket. The charity doesn’t exist.
scams.avoidance: Politely decline with ‘Non, merci’ and keep walking without breaking stride. Never sign anything on the street; legitimate charities don’t solicit signatures on promenades. Keep your hands occupied with bags or phone so you can’t take the clipboard. Genuine charities have websites, offices, and don’t rely on street solicitation.
scams.location: Grande Plage promenade, Place Clemenceau, near the casino, pedestrian shopping areas

scams.name: Remote Beach and Parking Lot Car Break-Ins
scams.description: You drive to one of Biarritz’s remote surf beaches for an afternoon in the water. You leave the rental car in the parking lot with your bags hidden in the trunk. But thieves stake out these beach parking areas, watching tourists head down to the water. Within minutes, they’ve smashed a window or popped the lock — and valuables ‘hidden’ in the trunk get found in under a minute.
scams.avoidance: Leave everything of value at your hotel; don’t bring anything to the beach you can’t carry into the water. Use paid, supervised lots rather than remote free parking whenever the option exists. If you must leave items in the car, load the trunk before you arrive, never in the lot. Don’t leave any bag visible, even if it contains nothing worth taking.
scams.location: Cote des Basques parking lot, Plage de la Milady parking, remote surf spot access roads, cliffside parking areas
